🧠 Cool Space Facts

Real facts from NASA!

☀️ Space Weather & DONKI

DONKI is NASA's big space-weather notebook. It tracks solar flares, and giant solar clouds called CMEs.

Solar flares are graded A, B, C, M, X — each letter is 10 times stronger. X is the biggest! A CME can take 1 to 3 days to travel from the Sun to us.

Source: NASA DONKI

🛡️ Radiation in Space

Earth's air and magnetic shield protect us. The Moon has almost no air and no shield like Earth's, so astronauts need strong walls and shelters there.

NASA's RadLab collects radiation measurements from the Space Station, the Moon, and even the Curiosity rover on Mars, so crews can stay safe.

Source: NASA RadLab / OSDR

🦴 Your Body in Space

Without gravity, bones can lose about 1% of their strength every month, and muscles get weak. Body fluid floats up to your head — puffy face!

That's why astronauts on the Space Station exercise about 2 hours a day on special treadmills, bikes, and weight machines.

Source: NASA Human Research

🌕 Moon & Mars Facts

One Moon daytime lasts about 14 Earth days — then 14 days of night! Solar power must survive the long night. It can be 127°C in the sun and −173°C at night.

Mars has only about 38% of Earth's gravity, and its air is mostly carbon dioxide — great for plants in a greenhouse, not for breathing. NASA's Mars Trek & Moon Trek maps show the real craters!

Source: NASA Solar System Treks

📚 NASA Data & Sources Used

All 7 official resources — and how each is used.

⚖️ The Big Trade-Off — the heart of this game

One outpost, three core resources — 💨 oxygen, 🔋 power and 🥬 food — always competing. Every helper in Moon Base Keeper spends power: growing food costs power the shield needs, fixing the shield costs power life support needs, and saving power today means oxygen can run low tomorrow. Every choice has a real cost — that trade-off is what a young player walks away understanding. Try it in the 🌱 Moon Base Keeper mission!

🏷️ How to read the labels: ● LIVE means fetched fresh from NASA while you play. Curated means real NASA facts our team researched and built in — true, but not live, and never labelled as live.

Two of these sources are fetched live while you play. The other five were researched by our team — their real facts, data and ideas are built into the missions, the training facts, and how the game is designed. If a live feed can't be reached, the game uses real backup NASA facts so it never breaks.

  1. 1

    NASA Open APIs● LIVE in the game

    How it's used: The “📡 Live from NASA” section on this Dashboard screen fetches today's Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD) and a real Mars rover photo live from api.nasa.gov every time the page opens. Each photo is shown with its NASA credit line. If the API is busy or you're offline, backup NASA facts appear instead — the game always works.

    Why we used it: So players see the REAL sky and the REAL Mars today — real photos make the training feel like a real mission, not a cartoon.

    api.nasa.gov

  2. 2

    DONKI — Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information● LIVE in the game

    How it's used: DONKI's live solar flare and geomagnetic storm reports from the last 30 days power the “Live Space Weather” panel at the top of the Space Weather Watch mission. The mission's motion quiz is built on DONKI's real space-weather science — solar flares and CMEs, graded A, B, C, M, X, and geomagnetic storms, graded G1 to G5 — alongside real spaceflight motions like launches, orbits, dockings and landings. Famous real storms from NASA's records are the fallback if the live feed is down.

    Why we used it: So Space Weather Watch trains with the Sun's REAL behaviour right now — real flares and storms decide what a crew must watch for.

    ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/tools/DONKI

  3. 3

    NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR)Curated facts — not live

    How it's used: We researched OSDR's astronaut-health studies on how the body changes in space — bone loss of about 1% a month, weaker muscles, and fluid shifting toward the head. Those facts are the science behind the Exercise in Space mission (why astronauts train about 2 hours a day) and the body-and-training facts in the “Cool Space Facts” cards and mission results.

    Why we used it: So Exercise in Space is built on what REALLY happens to astronaut bodies — the bone and muscle changes are why the workout mission exists.

    osdr.nasa.gov

  4. 4

    RadLab — Radiation Dosimetry DataCurated facts — not live

    How it's used: RadLab collects real radiation measurements from the Space Station, the Moon, and Mars instruments like Curiosity's RAD detector. We used its radiation facts to design the radiation-shield decisions in Moon Base Keeper — keeping the shield meter strong, fixing it before storms, and sheltering inside — and the radiation facts in the “Cool Space Facts” cards.

    Why we used it: So the shield decisions in Moon Base Keeper and Space Weather Watch use REAL radiation measurements — the danger and the dose are real, not made up.

    visualization.osdr.nasa.gov/radlab

  5. 5

    Mars Trek (NASA Solar System Treks)Curated facts — not live

    How it's used: Mars Trek's real maps of Mars — built from spacecraft data — gave us the Mars terrain and mission facts behind this game's Mars mission setting: Gale Crater where Curiosity landed, Mars's thin carbon-dioxide air, and its gravity at about 38% of Earth's. These appear in the Mars rover photo card, the “Moon & Mars Facts” card, and the game's mission briefings.

    Why we used it: So the Mars outpost choice uses REAL Mars maps and landing-site conditions — where a base could really land, and what it would really face.

    trek.nasa.gov/mars

  6. 6

    Canadian Space Agency (CSA) — Space Resources for STEM & Youth OrganizationsCurated guide — not live

    How it's used: The CSA's space resources for STEM and youth organizations shaped this game's training structure and kid-friendly mission design: short hands-on missions, a 7-day cadet-to-commander training path, badges for each skill, big tap-friendly controls, and simple language for ages 7–12 — learning by doing, the way youth space programs teach.

    Why we used it: So the training is designed the way real youth space programs teach — short, hands-on missions that kids aged 7–12 can actually finish and learn from.

    asc-csa.gc.ca — Youth & Educators

  7. 7

    Canadian Space Agency (CSA) — Food Production on the Moon ToolkitCurated facts — not live

    How it's used: The CSA's toolkit on growing food on the Moon — greenhouses, light, water recycling, and plants that feed crews far from Earth — supplied the researched facts behind the Grow Food system in Moon Base Keeper: growing lettuce adds food and oxygen but uses power, which is the trade-off at the heart of that mission.

    Why we used it: So growing food in Moon Base Keeper follows REAL Moon-greenhouse science — light, water and power costs included, which creates the game's Big Trade-Off.

    asc-csa.gc.ca — Food Production in Space

🏆 How We Meet the Challenge

Every requirement of the NASA Space Apps challenge “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” — and exactly what we built for it.

  1. 1

    1 · Astronaut training for kids aged 7–12, for the Moon or Mars

    What we did: Our game trains young astronauts through 6 missions — Spacewalk Training, Exercise in Space, Moon Base Keeper, Space Weather Watch, Moon Base Defender, and the Earth to Moon Journey — across a 7-day journey from Cadet to Mission Commander, with two levels: 🌱 Easy (ages 7–8) and 🚀 Commander Hard (age 10+).

  2. 2

    2 · Manage a lunar or Martian outpost and make real decisions

    What we did: In 🌱 Moon Base Keeper YOU are in charge of the outpost. You decide, second by second, what to fix, grow, charge and shelter — and your choices decide whether the crew of 4 stays safe for a whole Moon day. In the Journey you can also pick a Mars outpost landing site (see point 6).

  3. 3

    3 · Show one big trade-off clearly

    What we did: ⚖️ The Big Trade-Off: three core resources — 💨 oxygen, 🔋 power and 🥬 food — all compete for ONE power supply, and every choice has a real cost. Growing food spends power the shield needs. Fixing the shield spends power life support needs. Saving power today means oxygen can run low tomorrow. The trade-off is explained in Moon Base Keeper, on this Dashboard, and in the mission's science pop-up.

  4. 4

    4 · Life support, radiation shielding, power budgeting and food production

    What we did: All four are played, not just mentioned: life support — recycle air & water and keep the Oxygen meter alive in Moon Base Keeper; radiation shielding — keep the shield strong against RadLab-shaped solar-storm events in Moon Base Keeper and Space Weather Watch; power budgeting — every helper spends power, so you budget it like real money; food production — grow lettuce in a Moon greenhouse, based on the CSA Food Production toolkit and NASA's real Veggie space garden.

  5. 5

    5 · Communication delay

    What we did: In the 🚀 Earth to Moon Journey, Mission Control's messages arrive late on purpose: you watch the message travelling, it lands after a visible 1.3-second delay (the real Earth→Moon radio time), and the game explains that to Mars it would take up to ~22 minutes one way — so the pilot must decide without an instant reply, just like a real astronaut.

  6. 6

    6 · The Mars side — a Martian outpost, not just the Moon

    What we did: In the Journey you choose your Mars outpost from real Mars Trek landing sites — Jezero Crater (Perseverance), Gale Crater (Curiosity) or Elysium Planitia (InSight) — and each site's real conditions (freezing cold, thin air you can't breathe, stronger radiation, 38% gravity, a 24h 39m day called a sol) join your story when you fly past Mars. The Dashboard's “Live from NASA” shows a live real Mars rover photo of the world those rovers explore.

  7. 7

    7 · Real NASA data shapes the play — and why each dataset was used

    What we did: DONKI (LIVE) — today's real solar flares and storms power Space Weather Watch, because crews must react to the real Sun. OSDR (curated) — its astronaut-health finding (bones lose ~1% a month in microgravity) is why Exercise in Space exists. RadLab (curated) — its real radiation readings shape the shield and storm decisions, because the dose danger is real. Mars Trek (curated) — its real maps and site conditions make the Mars outpost choice true to Mars. NASA Open APIs — APOD & Mars Rover Photos (LIVE) — real photos of today's sky and Mars, so training feels like a real mission. CSA Space Resources for STEM & Youth (curated) — shaped our kid-friendly 7-day training design. CSA Food Production on the Moon Toolkit (curated) — its real greenhouse science (light, water, power costs) creates the food-vs-power trade-off. Full details are in tab 4, “NASA Data & Sources Used”. LIVE always means fetched fresh; curated means researched real facts — never labelled live.

  8. 8

    8 · Replayability — no two playthroughs the same

    What we did: Moon Base Keeper's surprise events are picked at random (solar storm, sunny spell, hungry crew, happy plants). Space Weather Watch shuffles its 7 motions and answers every game and reads live DONKI data, so the Sun itself changes the game. Spacewalk drops different tools in different places at different speeds every time, and the Journey's quiz questions come in a new order each flight.

  9. 9

    9 · Easy to play, easy to understand

    What we did: The whole game plays in the browser — no download, no account, no login — on phones, tablets and computers, with big tap-friendly buttons and voices reading the instructions aloud. Hard words are explained right where they appear, in plain words for ages 7–12: a radiation dose is invisible space energy soaking into your body, microgravity is floating where gravity feels almost zero, and a sol is one Mars day.

👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 For Parents & Teachers

What kids learn here, how to play together, and questions to talk about afterwards.

🧠 What kids learn in this game

Spacewalks: astronauts clip on a safety tether, tie down every tool, and move slowly and carefully outside the spacecraft.

Staying healthy: floating in space makes bones and muscles weak, so astronauts exercise about 2 hours a day — the game turns that into fast, fun tap practice.

Living on the Moon: a base must balance air, food, power and radiation shielding — and every helper uses power, so kids practise making trade-offs (choosing one thing means another thing waits).

Space weather: NASA's DONKI system watches the Sun. Flares are graded A, B, C, M, X — each letter ten times stronger — and crews shelter safely when storms come.

Thinking like a scientist: every mission opens with its real science (the Science Behind This pop-up), and every mission ends with one "Today I learned that…" sentence to remember.

Patience and planning: radio messages to the Moon take about 1.3 seconds each way, resources are shared across all 7 training days, and each day's real space weather changes one mission a little — just like real missions, no two days are the same.

👨‍👩‍👧 Playing together — families

Take turns as Mission Control: one person reads the instructions and cheers; the other plays. Swap every mission.

Use Switch Cadet: every family member can have their own saved cadet on the same device — tap Switch Cadet on the home screen.

Talk about the trade-offs: in Moon Base Keeper, ask "what did you save power for — and what ran low because of it?"

Short sessions work: one mission is one training day, about 1–3 minutes. Seven wins finish the training and earn the Commander certificate — a good screenshot to keep!

🏫 Playing together — classrooms

One device, whole class: show the game on a big screen, let the class vote on each move, and have one student tap the class's choice.

Crews of 3–4: give each crew member a job — Pilot (taps), Weather Officer (watches the Sun reports), Keeper (watches the meters), Reader (reads the science pop-ups aloud).

Connect it to lessons: the Dashboard's NASA Data & Sources tab lists the real NASA systems behind every mission (DONKI, RadLab, OSDR, Mars Trek), with links, if students want to explore further.

No accounts, no downloads: the game runs in the browser and saves progress only on the device being used.

💬 3 questions to talk about after playing

1. If you could only save ONE thing on a Moon base — air, food, or power — which would you save first, and why?

2. Astronauts exercise 2 hours a day so their bodies stay strong in space. What does YOUR body need every day to stay strong?

3. Messages to the Moon take time to arrive, so astronauts must decide some things by themselves. When is it good to decide by yourself — and when is it better to wait and ask?

🧑‍🚀 Spacewalk Training

❓ How to Play — Spacewalk

🕹️ You are floating outside the space station. Tools, supplies, asteroids and rocks are falling down from above!

  1. Press the ▶ START button — the mission begins right away!
  2. Move with the arrow keys / WASD, drag on the space board, or tap the arrow buttons.Move by tapping the on-screen D-pad (arrow buttons below the board) or drag on the space board.
  3. Move under the falling 🔧 tools and supplies to catch them. Collect 8 tools to win.
  4. Dodge the falling ☄️ asteroids and 🪨 rocks — 3 bumps and training ends!
  5. Finish before the 45 second timer runs out.
  6. 🔀 Every spacewalk is different — different tools drop, in different places, at different speeds, every time you play!

🎯 Goal: Collect 8 tools · 3 hearts · 45 seconds

🔧 Tools 0 / 8 ❤️ Hearts 3 ⏱️ Time 45s

❓ How to Play — Exercise

💪 In space, bones and muscles get weak without gravity. Exercise keeps astronauts strong!

  3. One pad will glow yellow. Tap that pad, fast!
  4. Tap the wrong pad, or tap too slowly, and the move changes.
  5. Get 10 good moves before the 45 second timer ends.

🧬 Real NASA Data Shapes This GameOSDR · Curated facts — not live

NASA's OSDR — its library of astronaut-health studies — found that in microgravity (floating in space, where gravity feels almost zero, so your body doesn't have to hold itself up) astronauts' bones lose about 1% of their strength every month and their muscles shrink.

That real finding is why this game exists: real astronauts exercise about 2 hours a day to fight it — and here, every good move you tap grows your astronaut's 🦴 Bone Power. Exercise isn't a bonus in space — it's survival!

🌱 Moon Base Keeper

❓ How to Play — Moon Base

🏠 You are in charge of the Moon base. Keep the whole crew safe for one full Moon day!

  1. Press the ▶ START button — the mission begins right away!
  2. Watch the 4 meters: air, food, power, and the radiation shield. They are always dropping!
  3. Tap the helper buttons to fill the meters back up.
  4. Careful! Growing food, fixing the shield, and recycling air all use power.
  5. Keep every meter above zero for 40 seconds to win.

🎯 Goal: Keep all 4 meters alive for 40 seconds

⏱️ Survived 0 / 40s 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 Crew 4 astronauts

⚖️ The Big Trade-Off — 3 core resources, ONE power supply!

Your base runs on just three core resources that are always competing — and every choice has a real cost:

💨 OXYGENthe air your crew breathes 🔋 POWERshared by EVERYTHING 🥬 FOODgrown under power-hungry lights

🌱 Grow lettuce → +Food, +Air … but −6 Power. Power spent growing food is power the shield and the air recycler can't use!

🛡️ Fix the shield → +Shield … but −5 Power. Spending power on shielding costs life support — the air recycler must wait.

💧 Recycle air & water → +Air … but −4 Power. And if you save power today by skipping recycling, oxygen can run low tomorrow — that is the trade-off!

☀️ Solar panels → +Power … but charging takes taps and time while the other meters keep dropping. There is never enough for everything at once — choosing what to save first IS the game, just like on a real Moon base.

🛡️ Real NASA data shapes this gameRadLab · Curated facts — not live
NASA's RadLab collects real radiation readings from space. They show the radiation dose — how much invisible space energy soaks into an astronaut's body, a bit like how much sunshine soaks into your skin — grows bigger during solar storms. That's why a storm event smashes your shield here, and why fixing the shield is worth its power cost.

🔀 Every Moon day is different! Surprise events are picked at random each game — a solar storm, a sunny spell, a hungry crew, or happy fast-growing plants — so no two days play the same.

👽 Moon Base Defender

❓ How to Play — Defender

👽 Friendly Moon Dust buddies — silly dust pals, NOT scary at all — are drifting toward your dusty, dark Moon Base! They start out stronger than you. Grow your light strength with NASA brain power, clear the dust, and make the base shine!

  1. Press the ▶ START button — the mission begins right away! You have 75 seconds.
  2. Each dust buddy shows the light strength it needs, like Needs 💪 4. You start with only Strength 💪 2.
  3. If your strength is big enough, tap the dust buddy to clear its dust away with light — it floats home clean and happy! ✨
  4. Need more strength? A NASA quiz question pops up! Every correct answer spreads light across the dark base, gives you +2 Strength, AND brings a good thing: extra oxygen 💨, food 🥬, power 🔋, a stronger shield 🛡️, or growing plants 🌱.
  5. A wrong answer gives no strength and no light — but don't worry, you can keep playing and try the next question!
  6. If a dusty buddy reaches the base, it makes the base dustier and dims the Base Light. Clear 10 buddies and answer 4 questions correctly to win — a bright, clean, shining base! The timer pauses while you answer — take your time reading.

🎯 Goal: Clear 10 dust buddies · 4 correct answers · A bright, clean, shining base · 75 seconds

🚀 Earth to Moon Journey

❓ How to Play — Journey

📖 A story adventure in 2 stages! Fly through a sky full of stars and planets to the Moon, dodge falling asteroids, meet the friendly Moon Friends, help them tidy up, and fly safely home.

  1. Press the ▶ START button — your journey begins right away!
  2. Stage 1 · Fly to the Moon: steer your spaceship from Earth to the Moon. First, answer the stage's quick quiz question to launch! Then a big 5-4-3-2-1 take-off countdown — your ship starts right on Earth, flames roaring, and Earth shrinks smaller and smaller behind you as you fly up through the sky into space! The flight takes a little while — about 15 seconds of flying to the middle of the journey, then about 16 more seconds on to the Moon — so enjoy the stars, planets and space scenery all around you!
  3. 📡 Mission Control messages arrive LATE! Radio waves take about 1.3 seconds to travel from Earth to the Moon, so Mission Control can never answer you instantly — watch the message panel under the start button. Real astronauts must decide by themselves while they wait!
  4. 🔴 Pick your Mars outpost! Under the start button, choose a real Mars landing site from NASA’s Mars Trek maps — its real conditions join your story when you fly past Mars.
  5. Dodge the asteroids! Asteroids and rocks fall down during the flight. Steer away from them! If one hits you, do not worry — you simply respawn (pop back to a safe spot) and keep flying. Asteroids can never crash you out — but watch the ⏱️ Moon clock: reach the Moon before it runs out, or the mission ends and you try again!
  6. In the middle of the flight, something goes wrong — a friendly warning light! Your ship stops, and spare parts (🔧 ⚙️ 🔋) float past. Steer into a part to collect it, then answer its NASA question — a correct answer installs the part! Collect and install 3 parts (3 correct answers) to fix the spaceship. Then keep flying to the Moon!
  7. You made it! When you reach the Moon, listen — a proud voice will say “Well done!” Then Stage 2 · Moon Friends Clean-Up: land, meet the bouncing Moon Friends, and answer the stage's quick quiz question to join the clean-up.
  8. The Moon is dusty! Tap a dust pile, answer its question, and clean it with light. 3 correct answers finish the cleaning.
  9. Then it is time to go home — a swirling star portal opens and teleports you back to Earth in one second! No long flight home!

🎯 Goal: Fly to the Moon before the Moon clock runs out (dodge the asteroids!) · 3 correct answers fix the ship · 3 more clean the Moon · 5-4-3-2-1 countdown · Teleport home through the star portal!

🗺️ Stage 1 · Fly to the Moon 🧠 Correct 0 / 3 ⏱️ Moon clock 60s 🚀 Earth → Moon

📡 Mission Control — Messages Arrive with a REAL Delay!

Radio messages zoom at the speed of light — the fastest anything can go — but space is enormous. A message from Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon… and up to about 22 minutes one way to reach Mars! So there is no instant reply: astronauts must think and decide by themselves while the answer is still travelling.

📭 No message yet — start the journey and watch this panel. When Mission Control sends a message, you'll see it travelling…

🔴 Choose Your Mars Outpost!Mars Trek · Curated facts — not live

The challenge isn't only the Moon — one day, this same crew flies on to a Martian outpost! Pick a real landing site from NASA's Mars Trek maps. Its real conditions will join your story — and on Mars you'd face the same Big Trade-Off (air, power, food) under a freezing, dusty sky. A Mars day is called a sol — one sol lasts 24 hours and 39 minutes, a little longer than an Earth day!

Tap a site to see its real Mars Trek conditions! Then watch for Mars on your flight — and see a ● LIVE real Mars rover photo in the Dashboard's “Live from NASA”.

      🧠 What I Learned

      • Spacewalks: astronauts clip on a safety tether, collect their tools, and watch out for space junk.
      • Staying healthy: exercise about 2 hours a day fights bone loss (about 1% a month) and keeps muscles strong.
      • Living on the Moon: a base must balance air, food, power and radiation shielding — every helper uses power.
      • Space weather: NASA's DONKI tracks solar flares (A–X) and storms, and crews shelter inside until the Sun is calm.
      • Defending the base: brain power is a superpower — correct NASA answers built your strength and earned oxygen, food, power and shield power-ups while you cleared the friendly Moon Dust buddies and lit up the Moon base.
      • Earth to Moon: a real trip to the Moon takes about 3 days each way — crews steer carefully, fix problems with brain power and Mission Control's help, and helping friends tidy up makes every place better.

      🧠 What I Learned

      Your astronaut report card

      🧑‍🚀 Spacewalks

      —

      Astronauts wear a tether so they don't float away, and train in giant pools on Earth because floating in water feels like floating in space!

      💪 Staying Healthy

      —

      Exercise in space fights bone loss (about 1% a month!) and keeps muscles and the heart strong for the trip home.

      🌱 Living on the Moon

      —

      Plants are heroes: NASA's Veggie garden on the Space Station grows lettuce that gives food AND cleans the air. Every helper on a base uses power — that's the big trade-off!

      ☀️ Space Weather

      —

      DONKI tracks flares (A–X) and CMEs. When a storm comes, the safest place is inside, behind shielding — spacewalks wait for a calm Sun.

      👽 Moon Base Defender

      —

      Real Moon dust is sharp, sticky and clings to everything — NASA studies it to keep bases and suits clean. In this bonus mission, correct answers are power: they build strength and refill oxygen, food, power and shields.

      🚀 Earth to Moon Journey

      —

      Apollo 8 flew all the way to the Moon and back in 1968! A real Moon trip takes about 3 days each way. In this story mission, you steered the ship, fixed a problem with NASA brain power, and helped the Moon Friends clean up.
